name: Pahlavism
summary: Pahlavism is the official ideology the Pahlavi monarchy built around Mohammad Reza Shah in the 1960s and 1970s: hereditary monarchy as the nation's guide and driver of state-led modernisation (the White Revolution, land reform, women's suffrage, literacy and health corps), nationalism rooted in ancient Persia, a curbed clergy, and a ruler who controlled parliament and in 1975 merged the parties into one.
scope: The profile covers Mohammad Reza Shah's regime ideology from the 1953 settlement to 1978, centred on the White Revolution of 1963, the 2,500-year celebration and the 1975 Resurgence Party, as the FRUS assessment, which uses the term, describes it. It leaves out Reza Shah's earlier nationalism, which scholars say lacked a stated programme, and today's Iranian constitutional monarchists. Answers rest on the regime's record and the Shah's recorded statements; the Shah's four-volume 1967 Pahlavism work and Shakibi's scholarship were not obtainable.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The Shah held that monarchy ensures the country's stability and affirmed it at his coronation and the 2,500th-anniversary celebration; the Embassy booklet presents the Shahanshah as the focal point of the nation.

strong-leader.rationale: The Shah dissolved a parliament that had gutted land reform and enacted it by decree, then governed as the final authority in domestic and foreign policy.

one-party-rule.rationale: In 1975 the Shah merged the parties into the Resurgence Party and required loyalty to monarchy, constitution and revolution, but the party's own ideology was left undefined and earlier practice was controlled multi-party politics.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Parliament was brought under tight control, its candidates approved by the Shah and some winners specified by him; he declared himself legislative head of state.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The Shah personally decided military purchases and force structure, appointed ministers and was the final authority on key appointments.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The Shah ruled by decree and left the Majlis dissolved for over two years despite the constitution's one-month limit, while professing loyalty to the constitution.

leader-cult.rationale: Towns carried statues of the Shah and his father, mass rallies displayed giant portraits and banners of his quotations, and the booklet says he personalised the revolution.

dynastic-succession.rationale: The dynasty's continuation through a Crown Prince was a goal of the Shah, who was himself heir to his father, and the booklet frames the Pahlavi succession as the nation's order.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: A doctrine built on a hereditary crown and dynasty could not hold that hereditary titles and privileges be abolished.

elective-rulers.rationale: The Shah's monarchy rests on inheritance of the throne, so choosing rulers by election contradicts it.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The head of state is a hereditary Shahanshah, not elected directly by the people.

democracy-best.rationale: The Shah selected candidates, specified winners and ended the multi-party system, so the record rejects free competitive voting as the basis of government.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Domestic opposition was silenced by imprisonment or co-option, and in 1975 those who rejected the three loyalties were told to leave or face prison as traitors.

land-redistribution.rationale: The Shah distributed land of over 50,000 villages and 17,000 estates to the cultivators, beginning with his own property, and called the reform a pillar of the revolution.

bound-labor.rationale: The landlord-peasant system was uprooted to free the farmer from the yoke of feudalism, the opposite of binding farmers to land and a lord.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Land went to individual cultivators and state-owned shares were to be sold to workers, farmers and the public, though state heavy industry and agro-industrial units stayed.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: Land was given to its cultivators as owners, the reverse of state ownership of all land, though forests and water were nationalised.

land-use-tenure.rationale: The reform aimed to invest cultivators with the freedom and responsibility of land ownership rather than temporary tenure of communal land.

collective-farming.rationale: The booklet lists farm cooperatives and agro-industrial units alongside individual land-owning farmers, so the programme mixed forms.

national-resource-control.rationale: Oil, forests and water were nationalised, and the Shah bargained hard with the oil consortium for more revenue.

public-ownership.rationale: The petroleum industry, forests and water were nationalised and key heavy industries stayed in state hands, while other state shares were to be sold off.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Development plans set outlays and priorities for industry and infrastructure, and the state owned the industrial units whose shares it later sold.

experts-over-public.rationale: The Shah favoured technocrat ministers with specialised training and no independent political ambitions, in a system closed to popular politics.

women-suffrage.rationale: The Shah's electoral reform granted universal suffrage to women, and he arranged for women deputies to be elected to the Majlis.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The Shah continued his father's course of removing clerical political power and acted forcefully against opposed clergy, though he courted pliable clerics and publicly showed piety.

clerical-rule.rationale: The Shah exiled Khomeini and jailed opposed clergy whose doctrine made the state their executive arm.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The Shah explicitly refused the role of a ceremonial symbol of unity and directed policy, appointments and parliament.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: In 1961 he dissolved the Senate and the Majlis over charges of rigged elections and ruled by decree for over two years.

separated-powers.rationale: The Shah described himself as executive, legislative and judicial head of state when announcing the 1963 reforms.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Land reform and other programmes were put into effect by royal decree rather than through the standing legislative process.

direct-votes.rationale: The Shah sent his reform programme to a popular referendum in January 1963 to bypass the landlord-dominated parliament.

state-harmful.rationale: A state-led modernisation under a monarch directing government rejects the claim that the state is unnecessary and harmful.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The Shah's state ran land reform, literacy, health corps, development plans and industry, far beyond defence, justice and property.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The regime centralised provincial authority, built state forces and set up state Houses of Equity, leaving no room for private courts or defence.

decide-locally.rationale: Reza Shah began and the present Shah continued bringing provincial administration under central control, making him the major locus of power.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The Shah gave political activity low priority behind development and in 1975 demanded unity behind the revolution toward the great civilization.

gradual-change.rationale: The booklet calls the programme a sudden, radical change and the Shah chose a radical rather than gradual reform of land and society, while keeping order and property.

national-rebirth.rationale: The booklet describes Iran as a giant awakening from a long sleep to regain its historic greatness through radical reform, and the 1975 party was named the Resurgence Party.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: The Shah celebrated the 2,500th anniversary of the monarchy's founding by Cyrus and the booklet says the Shahanshah has personified national unity since Cyrus.

nation-first.rationale: The Shah defined his policy as national independence, doing what best serves the interests of Iran, though he also pursued cooperation in the UN and with neighbours.

military-superiority.rationale: The Shah sought air and naval power able to destroy neighbouring regimes on their own ground and to make Iran an Indian Ocean power.

empower-police-military.rationale: The Shah's record is a large arms programme and priority to air, army and navy forces.

collective-defense.rationale: Iran belonged to the 1955 regional collective-defence pact and had bilateral defence agreement with the United States.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: The record is alignment with the United States through the 1955 pact and bilateral agreements, and the Shah called the two close friends.

avoid-permanent-military-alliances.rationale: Iran stayed in the 1955 collective-defence pact and the bilateral defence agreement with the United States.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Iran kept its alliance with the United States and its regional pact, and its US military mission advised its forces.

defeat-communism.rationale: The Shah declared friendly relations with all nations regardless of their systems and applauded US-Soviet agreement, though he opposed Soviet clients as threats.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Iran declared it rejects war as national policy, yet the Shah wanted forces able to strike enemies first on their own territory.

non-intervention.rationale: The stated policy is non-interference in other countries' domestic affairs, but the Shah also pledged to keep radicals out of the Gulf and to act in the region.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Iran planned eight nuclear power plants of 8,000 megawatts and the Shah said he hoped for atomic power plants within five years.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: The Shah led the call for a nuclear-weapon-free zone in the Middle East, backed by a UN vote.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: The Shah declared that Iran is not an atomic power and does not intend to become one.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: The Shah repeatedly said it is the moral responsibility of those who can to bridge the gap between rich and poor nations, and Iran gave aid to India, Pakistan, Egypt and others.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: The Shah proposed a new international institution with equal votes for developing countries, drawing on the World Bank to lend easy-term money to them.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: The Shah welcomed foreign banks and companies, saying they were most welcome as Iranian projects needed great foreign capital.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: The Shah said Iran cannot sit on its oil but must move it into world markets and maintained oil sales and export development.
